transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

I came in because I feel like I worry about everything lately—my clients, the market, my family, money, even whether moving to the condo was the right decision. It just feels like it’s more worry than the situations really call for.
How long have you been feeling this way—has this constant worrying been going on for several months, or did it start more recently after a specific event?
It’s been about a year and two months now. It started after I sold the house I’d lived in for a long time and moved into the condo.
Over this past year, have you also noticed feeling persistently sad, down, or losing interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed a persistent sadness or anything like that.

Do you have any medical conditions—like thyroid problems, heart issues, or other illnesses—or are you taking any medications, supplements, or substances that started around the same time your worrying began?
I’m not sure—I hadn’t really connected it to any medical issue or anything I started taking.
Along with the worrying, have you noticed physical symptoms like feeling restless or on edge, muscle tension, fatigue, or trouble concentrating on most days during this past year?

Yes. By the end of the day, my neck and shoulders feel really tight, like I’ve been bracing myself all day. And I catch myself clenching my jaw sometimes, especially driving between listings or sitting at my desk.
When you notice yourself worrying about these things, do you find it hard to stop or control the worry once it starts?
Yes, it is. Even if I tell myself, “Parin, this isn’t urgent,” one thing just leads into another. Then I realize I’ve spent half an hour going over little details I meant to just let go.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple domains (work, finances, family, decisions) persisting for over a year, longer than 6 months required for GAD. Associated physical symptoms include muscle tension (neck/shoulder tightness, jaw clenching) and difficulty controlling worry. Depressive symptoms (sadness, anhedonia) were explicitly denied, ruling out a primary mood disorder. No medical or substance cause was identified. While onset followed a life transition (selling house/moving), the worry is broad-based and chronic rather than restricted to adjustment to that specific stressor, favoring GAD over adjustment disorder.
